newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler-UAW pact cements pattern for GM showdown.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler-UAW pact cements pattern for GM showdown.

text.p: Now that the United Auto Workers union has signed similar labour pacts with Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp., industry giant General Motors Corp. will have a tougher time resisting the union's pattern.

Chrysler's deal with the UAW, signed on Sunday, cemented the pattern set by Ford, which includes guaranteed employment levels for the next three years and generous improvements in wages, benefits and pensions. It also allows the companies to pay lower wages to workers in new parts businesses they enter.

Ford's UAW workers ratified the pact by an overwhelming margin, the union said Monday, with 90 percent of votes from production workers approving the pact. Skilled trades workers ratified the contract by an 83 percent margin.
"Is there a pattern that's been set? The answer is yes," UAW President Stephen Yokich said on Sunday.
GM, the union's most difficult target, is expected to try to resist terms of the Ford and Chrysler agreements that would restrict its ability to shrink its domestic hourly work force.
Industry analysts estimated that GM needs to cut 50,000 to 60,000 hourly jobs through attrition to become competitive -- nearly as many as Chrysler's entire 66,000-member UAW hourly work force.
Currently, GM has about 215,000 hourly UAW employees. Ford agreed to guarantee jobs for 95 percent of its 105,000 UAW workers.
Talks with GM continued, but were expected to do so at a slower pace until after the union briefs local leaders on the Chrysler deal on Thursday.
Yokich has repeatedly indicated that he is willing to recognise GM's needs in the contract but has not indicated how far he is willing to go to help the world's largest automaker.
"I think times do change and you have to work more together," he said on Sunday. "We're in a competitive market -- it's a worldwide market."

But Yokich may have a difficult time selling a more lenient deal to rank-and-file GM workers worried about losing their jobs, said Dale Brickner, associate director of Michigan State University's School of Labour Relations.
With improving profits, strong truck sales and a massive number of new models set for launch, GM's cries of poverty ring hollow to many workers, Brickner said.

"Out in the trenches, no one really believes that GM is in trouble. These guys are working incredible overtime hours," Brickner said. "Yokich is dealing with that perception that he can't let GM off the hook."

Dean Witter analyst Ronald Glantz said he believes GM can afford to sign the Ford pact because it does not explicitly restrict the shifting of work to outside suppliers and offers sufficient room to adjust work forces at individual plants and during economic downturns.
"I anticipate GM will fuss and protest and eventually sign something close to what Ford and Chrysler signed," Glantz said.

One area for special consideration is the fate of two U.S. parts plants that GM has put up for sale, which employ nearly 2,100 UAW workers. The automaker is negotiating to sell the door hardware plant in Flint, Mich., and an interior trim plant in Livonia, Mich., to an unidentified buyer in a deal that also would include two Canadian plants that employ 3,300 members of the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union.
UAW officials in Flint have identified the buyer as Joseph, Littlejohn & Levy, a New York-based investment firm that owns other auto parts companies.

The CAW has resisted the sale of the Canadian plants, making them a major issue in its negotiations with GM, and is threatening to strike starting on Friday. The UAW has said little about the facilities.
The two unions have coordinated their bargaining moves in the past, and appear to be continuing to do so.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove said he has received assurances from Yokich that the UAW will not set a strike deadline in the United States while the CAW is still bargaining.
"He assured me that will not happen," Hargrove said. "He will not do anything that will interfere with our bargaining."
